title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
Ecological & Conservation Context
  
  
    Understanding how the world's largest fish uses tropical reef corridors, why satellite tags show surface bursts and deep-water gaps, and why international protection matters.

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
section: 1. Filter-Feeding Giants in a Tropical Ocean
text:
1. Filter-Feeding Giants in a Tropical Ocean
As the world’s largest living fish (Rhincodon typus), whale sharks are ectothermic (cold-blooded) filter feeders that navigate warm tropical and subtropical seas in search of dense prey patches:

Spawning Aggregation Hotspots: During late spring and austral summer (November–February), whale sharks gather along outer reefs of the northern Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea to feed on zooplankton blooms and mass fish and coral spawning events.
Surface Thermoregulation: After diving into deep, cooler ocean layers to forage, whale sharks return to sun-warmed surface waters to warm their bodies — creating the exact windows when fin-mounted satellite tags break the surface and uplink GPS locations.

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
2. Cross-Border Ocean Roaming
The trajectories on the Tracking Patterns map show that Coral Sea whale sharks do not stay inside a single reef or national boundary:

From Reef Shelves to Deep Basins: Tagged individuals travel across deep oceanic trenches between Queensland’s continental shelf, remote Coral Sea seamounts, and Papua New Guinea waters.
Subadult Male Dominance: Like many coastal whale shark aggregations worldwide, a large share of the tagged Coral Sea individuals are immature and subadult sharks using productive shelf edges to fuel rapid growth before dispersing into the wider Indo-Pacific.

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
section: 3. Why Satellite Telemetry Matters for Conservation
text:
3. Why Satellite Telemetry Matters for Conservation
Whale sharks are listed as Endangered globally on the IUCN Red List due to vessel strikes, fisheries bycatch, and changing ocean temperatures:

Pinpointing High-Risk Shipping Lanes: High-density tracking paths reveal where seasonal surface-feeding hotspots overlap with commercial shipping corridors along northeastern Australia and Papua New Guinea.
Protecting Connected Marine Parks: Because individual sharks like Megashark and Ali roam across hundreds of kilometers over multiple years, effective conservation depends on linking Australia’s Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea Marine Parks with neighboring Pacific protections.

title: About the Whale Shark & Beluga Whale Graphic
text:
Methodology & Data Guide
  
  
    Understanding the axes and interactive controls behind the visualization.

title: About the Whale Shark & Beluga Whale Graphic
text:
How to Read the Axes

Horizontal Axis (X-Axis) — Observation Date Span Elapsed (Days Since First Sighting):
Measures how many days have passed since that specific individual shark (or the Beaufort Sea mooring) was first recorded. Placing every track on a “Days Since First Sighting” scale lets us directly compare observation durations even when the recordings occurred in different calendar years.
Vertical Axis (Y-Axis) — Cumulative Spotting / Tracking Count:
Counts each new detection in chronological order (\(1, 2, 3, \dots, N\)). A steep upward curve means frequent detections over a short period, while a flatter curve means detections were spread out over a longer time span.
Color Grouping:
Dark teal points represent Whale Shark Trackings (Coral Sea) and light blue points represent Beluga Whale Detections (Beaufort Sea).

title: About the Whale Shark & Beluga Whale Graphic
text:
Using the Interactive Controls

Top Filter Sliders & Dropdown: Filter the points in real time by elapsed days, cumulative spotting count, or select a single named Whale Shark or the Beluga Whale dataset.
Timeframe View Menu (Top-Left of Plot): Switch between the full 4,006-day span, a log-scale X-axis that spreads short and long tracks evenly, or zoomed-in views of the 0–400 day overlap window.
Bottom Range Slider: Drag the handles at the bottom of the plot to zoom dynamically into any window of elapsed days.

title: Discover the Profiles of Each Individual Whale Shark Tracked
text:
Key Findings & Graph Breakdown
  
  
    This project analyzes 2,391 whale shark (Rhincodon typus) observations in Australia's Coral Sea collected by the Biopixel Oceans Foundation and James Cook University. The dataset combines 2,255 satellite transmissions from 18 individually named sharks along the Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea reefs with 136 opportunistic sightings recorded from 2007 to 2018. Explore the profiles below to see each shark's trajectory, deep-water plateaus, and seasonal surges.

  Megashark (Tag ID: 252324)
  
    Male · Immature
    423 Transmissions
    Span: 13.0 Months (2023-11-30 to 2024-12-31)
    Min. Distance: ~6,073 km
    Latitudes: 16.5°S to 9.7°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Forms the tallest trajectory on the scatter plot (reaching 423 cumulative detections). After climbing steeply over its first few summer months, it flattens across a 49-day mid-year gap before surging strongly again between Months 10 and 13.
    Ecological Takeaway: Shows classic seasonal cycling — frequent surface foraging during back-to-back austral summers separated by deeper offshore winter roaming across more than 6,000 km of the Coral Sea.
  



  Alexios (Tag ID: 178953)
  
    Male · Immature
    357 Transmissions
    Span: 5.2 Months (2021-12-05 to 2022-05-12)
    Min. Distance: ~4,307 km
    Latitudes: 18.1°S to 11.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Rises rapidly and smoothly to 357 detections in just over 5 months (~2.3 transmissions/day) with no silent gap longer than 13 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Indicates sustained surface and upper-water-column activity as this immature male traveled over 4,300 km along the outer Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea basin from summer into autumn.
  



  Ali (Tag ID: 178954)
  
    Female · Immature
    273 Transmissions
    Span: 25.3 Months (2021-12-06 to 2024-01-15)
    Min. Distance: ~11,378 km
    Latitudes: 18.6°S to 7.9°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Stretches farthest right among all tagged sharks (25.3 months / >2 years), advancing in staircase-like seasonal bursts separated by gaps of up to 73 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: One of only two confirmed females in the tagged cohort and the dataset's long-distance marathoner, logging over 11,300 km between central Queensland latitudes and waters near Papua New Guinea.
  



  Sharpie (Tag ID: 252325)
  
    Male · Immature
    261 Transmissions
    Span: 3.2 Months (2023-12-01 to 2024-03-07)
    Min. Distance: ~1,544 km
    Latitudes: 13.5°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: One of the steepest initial slopes on the chart, packing 261 locations into 97 days (~2.7 uplinks/day) with a maximum gap of only 10 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Stayed within a relatively tight northern reef band (11.3°S–13.5°S), spending long periods basking and filter-feeding at the surface during peak summer plankton productivity.
  



  Juanita (Tag ID: 172900)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    204 Transmissions
    Span: 4.3 Months (2023-11-03 to 2024-03-14)
    Min. Distance: ~2,642 km
    Latitudes: 16.6°S to 8.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Climbs steadily from Month 0 to 204 detections across 4.3 months, punctuated by brief 1–3 week pauses (max gap 21 days).
    Ecological Takeaway: Tracked earlier in spring (early November) than most sharks and ranged widely across 8.5 degrees of latitude northward into the northern Coral Sea.
  



  GBR1 (Tag ID: 172899)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    177 Transmissions
    Span: 4.8 Months (2018-10-26 to 2019-03-21)
    Min. Distance: ~3,677 km
    Latitudes: 14.2°S to 6.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Exceptionally smooth, unbroken upward line over nearly 5 months — never going more than 4 days without a satellite uplink.
    Ecological Takeaway: Reached the northernmost latitude of any shark in the dataset (6.3°S in Papua New Guinea waters), proving cross-border movement across the northern Coral Sea.
  



  Beizam (Tag ID: 243952)
  
    Male · Subadult
    98 Transmissions
    Span: 2.2 Months (2023-12-02 to 2024-02-08)
    Min. Distance: ~1,846 km
    Latitudes: 17.2°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Steady 2.2-month climb to 98 detections across December–February with minimal transmission gaps.
    Ecological Takeaway: Notable as the only Subadult shark in an otherwise immature-dominated tagged group, cruising rapidly southward and offshore (~27 km/day) across nearly 6 degrees of latitude.
  



  Blancpain (Tag ID: 178957)
  
    Female · Immature
    73 Transmissions
    Span: 17.3 Months (2021-12-06 to 2023-05-16)
    Min. Distance: ~1,943 km
    Latitudes: 14.5°S to 8.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Features the most dramatic horizontal plateau on the entire plot — going silent for 276 consecutive days (~9 months) before resuming transmissions past Month 15.
    Ecological Takeaway: Along with Ali, one of only two tagged females; demonstrates how whale sharks can spend months foraging in deep or remote waters without long surface intervals before reappearing the next season.
  



  GBR2 (Tag ID: 176413)
  
    Male · Immature
    69 Transmissions
    Span: 2.9 Months (2019-11-17 to 2020-02-13)
    Min. Distance: ~2,675 km
    Latitudes: 15.1°S to 10.8°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Moderate 3-month summer curve reaching 69 uplinks with occasional 1–2 week diving gaps.
    Ecological Takeaway: Covered high daily mileage (~30 km/day average between pings), moving briskly across outer Coral Sea reefs during the 2019–2020 summer season.
  



  Infamis (Tag ID: 243954)
  
    Male · Immature
    66 Transmissions
    Span: 2.4 Months (2023-12-01 to 2024-02-12)
    Min. Distance: ~644 km
    Latitudes: 13.8°S to 12.2°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Compact 2.4-month summer trajectory rising to 66 detections near the base of the main summer cluster.
    Ecological Takeaway: Showed strong site fidelity within a narrow 1.6° latitude band along the northern Great Barrier Reef shelf edge rather than making an immediate long-distance crossing.
  



  Jaap (Tag ID: 178948)
  
    Male · Immature
    63 Transmissions
    Span: 1.3 Months (2019-11-19 to 2019-12-28)
    Min. Distance: ~255 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 11.6°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Steep short-duration curve reaching 63 locations within 39 days (~1.6 uplinks/day).
    Ecological Takeaway: Remained tightly localized around the Wreck Bay / northern reef aggregation hotspot during late November and December coral spawning.
  



  Halliday (Tag ID: 243955)
  
    Male · Immature
    53 Transmissions
    Span: 1.3 Months (2023-12-04 to 2024-01-12)
    Min. Distance: ~772 km
    Latitudes: 15.0°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Climbs cleanly to 53 detections over 39 days across December and early January.
    Ecological Takeaway: Unlike Jaap over the same 39-day span, Halliday traveled more than three times farther (~772 km), heading southward along the outer reef margin.
  



  Hugh (Tag ID: 243951)
  
    Male · Immature
    53 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 7 Days (2023-11-30 to 2023-12-07)
    Min. Distance: ~143 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 12.0°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Appears nearly vertical near Month 0, recording 53 high-frequency transmissions in just one week (~7.6 uplinks/day!).
    Ecological Takeaway: Captures intense, continuous surface feeding right after tagging before the tag ceased reporting or detached.
  



  Fifty_Fathoms (Tag ID: 178951)
  
    Male · Immature
    24 Transmissions
    Span: 1.2 Months (2021-12-05 to 2022-01-11)
    Min. Distance: ~868 km
    Latitudes: 14.6°S to 11.5°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Low, gentle 1.2-month curve reaching 24 transmissions over 37 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Despite fewer surface uplinks, covered nearly 870 km across 3 degrees of latitude — suggesting deeper travel with briefer surface intervals.
  



  Sapphire (Tag ID: 176409)
  
    Male · Immature
    24 Transmissions
    Span: 0.3 Months / 9 Days (2024-03-05 to 2024-03-14)
    Min. Distance: ~1,387 km
    Latitudes: 16.5°S to 12.7°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Short 9-day burst of 24 detections near the origin of the X-axis.
    Ecological Takeaway: Tracked in March (late summer/early autumn) rather than December, moving rapidly across wide Coral Sea distances in just over a week.
  



  Andrew (Tag ID: 243953)
  
    Male · Immature
    18 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 5 Days (2023-12-01 to 2023-12-06)
    Min. Distance: ~76 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 11.9°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Brief 5-day cluster of 18 transmissions right at Month 0.
    Ecological Takeaway: Represents short-term local foraging around the northern reef tagging site in early December before early tag loss or deep offshore departure.
  



  Dotti (Tag ID: 178949)
  
    Male · Immature
    10 Transmissions
    Span: 0.1 Months / 3 Days (2019-11-20 to 2019-11-23)
    Min. Distance: ~20 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Compact 10-point cluster at the bottom-left origin of the plot.
    Ecological Takeaway: Captures a 3-day snapshot of localized reef aggregation behavior at 12.2°S during the November 2019 tagging expedition.
  



  Ambitious (Tag ID: 176407)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    9 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 6 Days (2019-11-19 to 2019-11-25)
    Min. Distance: ~19 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 12.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Shortest tagged trajectory on the graph (9 uplinks across 6 days near Month 0).
    Ecological Takeaway: Like Dotti, illustrates both localized reef feeding at 12.2°S and a real-world challenge of marine telemetry — tags can shed early or stop reporting once a shark dives into deep water.

title: Discover the Profiles of Each Individual Whale Shark Tracked
text:
Peak Austral Summer Window (November–February)
Looking at the monthly bar chart on the Overview tab highlights a strong warm-season surge in the Coral Sea: transmissions climb dramatically starting in late spring and summer as whale sharks aggregate along outer reef shelf edges to feed near the surface on dense plankton blooms and coral/fish spawning events.

title: Discover the Profiles of Each Individual Whale Shark Tracked
text:
Mid-Year Offshore Dispersal (May–September)
Detection counts drop during the austral winter not because whale sharks vanish from the Pacific, but because individuals disperse widely across deep open-ocean basins and spend longer intervals foraging at depth where fin-mounted satellite tags cannot transmit through seawater.
